source.title: Code-Switching Curriculum Learning for Multilingual Transfer in LLMs
source.authors: Haneul Yoo; Cheonbok Park; Sangdoo Yun; Alice Oh; Hwaran Lee

record.file_problem: No apparent truncation or corruption; the full paper, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study varies training-corpus size and reports downstream benchmark performance, a different measure bearing on V6. It does not measure held-out cross-entropy or test parameter- or compute-scaling laws.
record.gate_note: Figure 3 varies the amount of monolingual training data and reports Multilingual MMLU performance. This is the only result bearing on a claim version. The other language-transfer and task results compare training methods without varying scale; they do not test the listed versions. No held-out pretraining-loss results are reported.
record.test_reason: Section 4.4 varies continued-pretraining data for Qwen 2 (1.5B) and reports MMLU accuracy. This is a weak, new-setting result on V6 (downstream performance rising with data scale). There are only four points from one model, values appear in the figure only, and no fit is made. The authors' phrase "following the scaling law" is an assertion, not a tested fit. No loss, parameter or compute scaling is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say performance in both languages rises with more monolingual data, "following the scaling law", but they fit no law. Their main point is that CSCL with less data beats conventional training with more, so CSCL suits low-resource languages. The Korean gap between methods narrows with more data, while the English gap stays constant.
record.recipe_differences: The study compares continued-training curricula and reports downstream task scores as data volume varies; it does not use the original sources' held-out cross-entropy scaling measurements or compute-optimal allocation procedure.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported Korean performance gap between CSCL and Ko-En decreases as monolingual corpus size increases, while CSCL consistently exceeds Ko-En in English.
record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The relevant scaling results are presented in Figure 3 without numerical values in the text, and uncertainty estimates are not stated. The experiment varies data volume for one model size and does not fit or evaluate predictive power laws.
record.rows_left_out: Other reported benchmark, generation, instruction-tuning, language, model-family, and safety results do not vary scale in a way that tests a listed version. Their results are described in Tables 1–12 and other sections; they are therefore not included as rows.

untested.parts: Parameter scaling; prediction from pretraining loss; any quantitative predictive fit or extrapolation.
No power-law fit in a continued-pretraining or transfer regime.

missing.what: MMMLU Ko/En for Qwen 2 (1.5B) at 1B total training data (Ko-En 37.7/53.0, CSCL 42.3/54.4; baseline 36.4/56.5). Compared with the 3B results in Table 6/7 (Ko-En 38.9/51.2, CSCL 49.4/52.3), this gives a second data-scaling comparison. In it, English falls as data grows.

record.verdict_notes: This is a method paper (code-switching curriculum); the scaling ablation is secondary. The evidence for V6 is weak: four points from one model, figure-only values, no uncertainty, and no fit. The data-size variable confounds changing the data ratio with changing the total.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or loss scaling with parameter count, tokens, or compute is measured.
No small-run loss fit is used to predict larger-run loss.
No fixed-compute allocation between parameter count and tokens is evaluated.
Architecture shape is not systematically varied at fixed parameter count to measure loss.
The study evaluates language transfer, but does not test whether the same power-law form holds for loss in other modalities or training regimes.
Only downstream Multilingual MMLU performance as monolingual training-data size varies is examined. The study does not test parameter scaling, loss-to-task prediction, or numerical predictive fits.
The study does not compare fitted loss exponents or compute-optimal allocations across setups or fitting choices.

rows.subject: Qwen 2 (1.5B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied monolingual corpus size in the Ko-En training method while keeping the two code-switching corpora fixed.
rows.baseline: figure only (baseline without further training, shown as a dotted line)
rows.note: The text says performance in Korean advances as more monolingual corpora are incorporated. The figure gives separate plotted values, but the paper text does not state their numbers.
rows.check: Values are figure only. The row shows only a monotonic rise over 1B–8B of monolingual data (3B–10B total). Predictability cannot be judged because no fit is given.

rows.subject: Qwen 2 (1.5B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied monolingual corpus size in CSCL while keeping the two code-switching corpora fixed.
rows.baseline: figure only (baseline without further training, shown as a dotted line)
rows.note: The text says performance in Korean advances as more monolingual corpora are incorporated. It also says the gap between CSCL and Ko-En decreases in Korean, and CSCL with smaller corpora can outperform conventional training with larger corpora. Individual plotted values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Values are figure only, and the rise is monotonic with no fit. The data-size variable is confounded: the code-switching phases stay fixed at 2B while monolingual data grows.

rows.subject: Qwen 2 (1.5B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied monolingual corpus size in the Ko-En training method while keeping the two code-switching corpora fixed.
rows.baseline: figure only (baseline without further training, shown as a dotted line)
rows.note: The text says performance in English advances as more monolingual corpora are incorporated. Separate plotted values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Values are figure only. The English scores sit near or below the untrained baseline (56.5 in Tables 5 and 12) because of forgetting. They rise with more monolingual data, which includes English.

rows.subject: Qwen 2 (1.5B)
rows.operation_detail: Varied monolingual corpus size in CSCL while keeping the two code-switching corpora fixed.
rows.baseline: figure only (baseline without further training, shown as a dotted line)
rows.note: The text says performance in English advances as more monolingual corpora are incorporated and that CSCL consistently exceeds conventional training in English. Separate plotted values are not stated in text.
rows.check: Values are figure only. The same forgetting caveat applies: the scores are relative to an untrained baseline that is higher.

relationships.condition: Qwen 2 (1.5B), Korean MMMLU, monolingual data 1B→8B, both Ko-En and CSCL
relationships.reason: Korean accuracy rises monotonically with added monolingual data in F3-KO-KOEN and F3-KO-CSCL. This shows only qualitative monotonicity; no fit is made.
relationships.display_finding: Korean accuracy increased monotonically under both Ko-En and CSCL, without a fitted predictive relationship.

relationships.condition: Qwen 2 (1.5B), English MMLU during language-transfer continued pretraining
relationships.reason: English rises with monolingual data in F3-EN rows. From the text (Table 12 vs Table 6), English MMMLU falls when total data goes from 1B to 3B: Ko-En 53.0→51.2 and CSCL 54.4→52.3. Throughout, it stays below the untrained baseline of 56.5, so the gain with data depends on the data mix.
relationships.display_finding: Increasing total data from 1B to 3B reduced English MMMLU from 53.0 to 51.2 for Ko-En and 54.4 to 52.3 for CSCL, below the 56.5 baseline despite gains with monolingual data.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
